summary: This document analyzes threats to telephone identity in the interconnected Internet and telephone network, where attackers can impersonate or hide calling numbers. It lists actors, their capabilities and the attacks, to guide the design of countermeasures.

eli5.summary: Before building a lock, you think about who might try to break in and how. This RFC does that for fake caller IDs, listing the troublemakers and tricks.

subtitle: A catalogue of who can impersonate a caller's phone number, how, and what that enables.

tldr.problem: Robocalling, voicemail hacking and similar abuse depend on being able to put someone else's calling telephone number on a call, and the telephone network offers no secure identity for that number.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out the actors (endpoints, intermediaries, attackers), assumes attackers can supply any calling number, and walks through the attacks and attack scenarios that countermeasures must address.
tldr.outcome: It is a threat model for the STIR work, not a solution, and it narrows the problem to verifying the calling number at call setup.

facts.label: Threat in scope
facts.value: Impersonating the calling number at call setup

today: RFC 7375 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the threat model that accompanies the problem statement in RFC 7340.

sections.title: Scope of the Threat
sections.content:
As the STIR problem statement (RFC 7340) explains, the main enabler of robocalling, vishing, swatting and related attacks is the ability to impersonate a calling party number. Robocallers prefer not to use a number that traces back to them, so they impersonate numbers not assigned to them.

The model covers only the rendering of a calling telephone number to the callee at call setup. It assumes this attack cannot be prevented: nothing stops an attacker from creating call setup messages with a chosen number. The solution space is therefore about letting terminating or intermediary elements tell authorized from unauthorized numbers so that policies can act on it.

Out of scope are impersonating a listener after setup (eavesdropping), changes to a call after it is established such as transfers, verifying the reached party's number back to the caller, and attacks specific to calling party names (Caller ID).
sections.eli5: The goal is not to stop people from writing a fake name on an envelope. It is to let the person receiving the letter check whether the name is real.

sections.title: The Actors
sections.content:
Endpoints are dumb devices (a simple dial pad, handset and ringer whose intelligence lives in the provider network), smart devices (programmable general-purpose computers such as smart phones), and automated terminals without a user, such as voicemail services that may grant different service based only on the calling number.

Intermediaries forward call signaling along the call path and may modify it. The model assumes no restrictions on those modifications. A gateway is an intermediary that translates signaling between protocols. Calls can be forwarded or retargeted and so end up somewhere the originator did not expect. Some gateways discard calling number data, for example by sending the number of the Primary Rate Interface line instead. In those cases authenticated data may be impossible, which is not itself an attack.

Attackers can create calls at will on the PSTN or over IP with any calling number, can capture and replay signaling they have seen, and have Internet access. Compromised intermediaries and stolen credentials are not considered.
sections.eli5: There are phones, the post offices in the middle that pass calls along, and the troublemakers. The troublemakers can write any return address they like and can copy old letters.

sections.title: The Attacks
sections.content:
Three attacks are described. In voicemail hacking, a service that grants access based on the calling number can be fooled by an attacker who impersonates the target's number. The same applies to banks, airlines, calling-card services and others that rely on the number alone. Countermeasures include treating calls with authenticated number data differently, for instance by requiring a PIN when it is absent.

In unsolicited commercial calling the robocaller needs only a plausible number, perhaps unassigned or not assignable, and may change it every call. Text messaging spam works similarly. One countermeasure is checking that the number is assigned. Because post-dial delay matters, cryptographic and network operations must be minimized. The expected effect is to force robocallers to either block their identity or use authenticated numbers traceable to them.

In telephony denial of service (TDoS), incessant calls tie up a target and impersonation hides the origin. Authenticated numbers let endpoints deprioritize unsigned calls during congestion. The RFC adds that this is unlikely to help against attacks on emergency responders, who are effectively obliged to answer every call.
sections.eli5: Fake caller ID lets crooks get into someone's voicemail, pester people with robot calls, or jam a phone line with calls. Checking that a number is real helps with the first two and with some of the third.

sections.title: Attack Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC gives four ways the chosen number reaches the callee, using SIP, WebRTC, Q.931 and SS7 signaling:

  • IP to IP: an attacker puts a chosen number in the From header field of a SIP INVITE.
  • PSTN to PSTN: a PBX sends a Q.931 SETUP with a chosen number, which the provider inserts into the SS7 calling party number field of the Initial Address Message.
  • IP to PSTN: an attacker uses a commercial WebRTC service and an Internet-to-PSTN gateway, which inserts the chosen number into the SS7 message.
  • IP to PSTN to IP: a SIP request crosses a gateway into the PSTN and then a second gateway back into an H.323 network, carrying the chosen number the whole way.

Solution-specific attacks are left to later work, but the RFC lists some to consider, such as replaying or removing parts of messages for in-band solutions and provisioning false data into datastores for out-of-band ones. It also says credentials issued to carriers or national authorities must be limited to numbers under their purview.
sections.eli5: Whether the call travels over the internet, the old phone network or both, the fake number just gets copied along from one stage to the next, so every route has the same weakness.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's own security section is a single sentence: the document provides a threat model and is therefore entirely about security. All its content on risks is in the sections on actors, attacks and attack scenarios.

It does note limits that affect how a future solution is judged. The model does not consider operators of intermediaries who deliberately discard valid identity or send falsified identity, and it assumes that secure design and operation of systems is necessary for any countermeasure to work.
sections.eli5: This whole document is about what could go wrong, so there is no separate warning label at the end.

data.title: Carriers of the forged calling number
data.code:
IP-IP:       SIP INVITE, From header field
PSTN-PSTN:   Q.931 SETUP -> SS7 IAM, CgPN field
IP-PSTN:     WebRTC service -> gateway -> SS7 IAM, CgPN field
IP-PSTN-IP:  SIP From -> SS7 IAM CgPN -> H.323 SETUP
